newsitem.title: FRANCE: Total denies Burma rights abuse claim.
newsitem.headline: Total denies Burma rights abuse claim.

text.p: French energy company Total SA on Wednesday denied a human rights group's allegations that its involvement in a gas pipeline project in Burma had caused abuses and said it would continue its investment.

The International Human Rights Federation (FIDH) said in a report issued earlier on Wednesday that Total had "knowingly closed its eyes to massive, systematic and violations of human rights and thus made itself an accomplice" in the construction of the pipeline.
Total, the leading international stakeholder in the project, said the report was based on second-hand information, including opposition reports.
"It does not contain a single new element which might cause Total to reconsider its position on this project," the company said in a statement.
"This gas pipeline project serves and will serve the interests of the people of Burma and of the region."
Total owns 31 percent of the 60 km (35 mile) pipeline designed to transport gas from the Yadana oilfield, 70 km (42 miles) off the Burmese coast in the Andaman Sea, to Thailand.
U.S. Unocal Corp is the second largest owner with 28 percent.

In its report, the FIDH said the Burmese army, in preparing for the pipeline project and guarding it, had "displaced the local population, used forced labour and committed violence such as rape and torture."
The army had also stepped up attacks on local rebel groups and carried out reprisals against civilian populations, it said.

The report echoed others issued by the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights and Amnesty International, which have denounced widespread violations under Burma's State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC).

Burmese democracy campaigner and Nobel Prize winner Aung San Suu Kyi singled out Total in an interview with French daily Le Monde in July, saying it had become the "strongest supporter" of Burma's military junta.

Reiterating its previous response to such accusations, Total argued the pipeline project had created hundreds of jobs and had brought advantages for the population including extra medical facilities, vaccination programmes and schools.
"This project will give this very poor country a chance to develop its natural resources and supply it with 30 years of energy which it desperately needs," Total said.
It added that the region where the pipeline is being built had known civil strife between ethnic groups and Burma's central government for half a century.
